t: How To Handle Students Who Will Ruin Your Day If You Hold Them Accountable day-if-you-hold-them-accountable/
q: You’ll have to give up your leverage and authority and treat them differently than everyone else.
So now this one student, all of eight years old—or four or thirteen—has you over a barrel and the best you can hope for is to ignore them and cross your fingers that they don’t become too disruptive.
How they handle it isn’t your concern. If they argue, don’t respond. If they throw themselves on the floor, leave them be.
And when they break another rule? Do it again. Follow your plan. Their reaction may be as bad as the first time—perhaps worse—but before long, if you stick with it, it will get better.

You see, when you offer your students real-world truth and acceptance, when you stop tiptoeing around them and instead show your faith in them and who they can become by never letting misbehavior go . . .

q: Summer provides an opportunity to push the reset button, to reflect on the previous year and make resolutions for the next.
Consistency in your behavior, in your interactions with students, in your speaking and temperament, and in your follow-through is critical to creating a happy, well-behaved classroom.
Every repeatable moment of the school day should be made into a routine your students can perform without your assistance.
Maintaining a calm, easygoing demeanor settles students, removes excitability, and gives you the effortless leadership presence your students will want to follow.

It’s about relationships. It’s about good instruction. It’s about being real and clear and direct. It’s about love and laughter.

t: How To Have Effective Classroom Management https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2014/06/14/how-to-have-effective-classroom-management/
q: Teachers who struggle with classroom management tend to head into the start of every school year with a wait and see approach.
It isn’t a jumbled, disparate, mix-up of strategies that have no business being in the same classroom together.
No, effective classroom management is deliberate and predictable—with success determined ahead of time.
It calls for you to go into each new school year knowing how to create a classroom your students will love being part of, where work habits, politeness, and independence develop naturally.
Beginning a new school year without a clear-cut vision and understanding of where you want to go and how you’re going to get there is a precarious game of chance.
You really can take a new group of students with vastly different personalities and behavior tendencies and transform them into the class you’ve always wanted.
x: A 'wait and see,' instinct-driven approach to classroom management is a gamble, not a plan.
Effective classroom management must be deliberate, proactive, and unified—not a mismatched grab-bag of borrowed strategies.

t: Why Shifting Responsibility To Your Students Can Change Everything dents-can-change-everything/
q: Teachers who struggle with classroom management tend to carry the weight of the world on their shoulders.
They’ve been conditioned to believe that their hovering presence and near-constant input is the only way to keep a lid on their classroom.
You see, the students in the above scenario behave the way they do because they receive too much attention.
They focus on teaching and modeling highly detailed expectations. They focus on showing precisely, step-by-step, what they want their students to do .
They shift the responsibility for carrying out their expectations in toto to their students. They take a step back and allow their students to succeed ( or fail ) all on their own.
Their expectations are backed both by individual and group consequences , but never by micromanagement.

By focusing on providing world-class instruction—the very essence of what it means to be a teacher—and then allowing your students to do their job, you can completely change the character of your classroom.
x: The fix is to teach and model expectations with great precision, then step back entirely and let students carry them out.

Linsin describes a common but unsustainable pattern of teachers who feel they must constantly walk, talk, correct, and remind students in order to keep a classroom functioning, contrasted with the disengaged, impulsive…
He argues the constant attention is itself the cause of student immaturity and low ownership, not the cure.
The fix is to teach and model expectations with great precision, then step back entirely and let students carry them out.
Students should be allowed to succeed or fail on their own once expectations are well taught, without rescue or reminders.
Real individual and group consequences back this system, but micromanagement and unnecessary help do not.
The piece closes by describing the transformation this produces—students who crave responsibility and rise to it, and a teacher who experiences a more joyful, masterful version of the job.
